AVALON CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  TUESDAY, JANUARY 18, 2022— 5:00 P.M.
  410 AVALON CANYON ROAD
  THIS VIRTUAL MEETING IS HELD PURSUANT TO AB 361

  In compliance with the Americans with Disability Act: if you need special assistance to participate in this
  meeting, please contact Denise Radde, City Clerk (310) 510-0220. Notification 48 hours prior to the meeting
  will enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to ensure accessibility to this meeting. (28 CFR 35.
  102-35.104 ADA Title ll) All public records relating to an agenda item on this agenda are available for the
  public inspection at the time the records are distributed to all: or a majority of all: members of the City Council.
  Such records shall be available at City Hall located at 410 Avalon Canyon Rd.
  Due to health recommendations from the Center for Disease Control and State of California Division of
  Occupational Safety and Health (CaI/OSHA), and the declared state of emergency wherein social
  distancing measures have been imposed or recommended: the CITY OF AVALON’S CITY COUNCIL
  and PLANNING COMMISSION MEETINGS SHALL GENERALLY BE AVAILABLE TO THE PUBLIC
  REMOTELY. The general pub//c may attend the meet/ny in the Counci/ Chambers however must adhere
  to socia/ distancing requirements and wear a mask or face covering at all times. The public is encouraged
  to watch and participate from the safety of their homes while practicing social distancing.

  Council Chambers are open to a maximum 30 members of the general public. Once the Council
  Chambers reach maximum occupancy, the general public may participate in Oral Communication and
  address the City Council on an agenda item in person by waiting in the City Hall Court Yard and entering
  the Chambers one at a time at the appropriate time. No one will be admitted into the Council Chambers
  who is ill or exhibiting symptoms of COVID-19. All individuals entering the Council Chambers must wear
  a mask or face covering at all times. Additionally, the general public may participate in Oral
  Communication and address the City Council on an agenda items by providing comments via e
  Comment. Please use the link below to provide comments via e-Comment.

ORAL COMMUNICATION
Members of the public may address the City Council at this time. No action will be taken on non-
agenda items at this meeting. Speakers should limit comments to two (2) minutes each.

CONSENT CALENDAR

1.  Minutes
  Although the live recording is the official record of public meetings, actions are prepared
  for the Council’s approval.
  Recommended Action
  Approve minutes from the January 4, 2022 regular City Council Meeting.

2.  Warrants
  Expenditures Submitted for Approval
  o Warrants in the amount of $290,270.90.
  o One payroll in the amount of $194,283.00.
  o Four electronic fund transfers totaling $169,962.23.
  Recommended Action
  Approve total expenditures for December 27, 2021 through January 7, 2021 totaling
  $654,516.13.

3.  Consideration of a Planning Commission Resolution Recommending City Council
  Adoption of the Annual Growth Policy for 2022
  The Avalon Municipal Code stipulates that the City Council, in conjunction with the
  Planning Commission, shall review the growth permitted in the preceding ten months,
  review the effects and demands of such development and any additional development
  upon the City’s natural resources, and determine, by resolution, the amount and type of
  growth the City will permit in the succeeding year, as well as City priorities for growth.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt a resolution establishing the City of Avalon’s Annual Growth Policy for 2022.

4.  Repair & Maintenance of City Floats 2 and 3 Located at the Cabrillo Mole
  Due to budgetary constraints and the COVID-19 pandemic, the City deferred
  maintenance on a number of infrastructure projects including the rehabilitation of Mole
  Floats 2 and 3. Mole Floats 2 and 3 are in need of repair and maintenance within the
  scope of work that is routinely and safely provided by Al Larson Boat Shop, a sole source
  vendor.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the Harbor Master to contract with Al Larson Boat Shop, a sole source
  vender, for the Repair and Maintenance of City Floats 2 and 3 for a sum not-to-exceed
  $249,999.00.
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
JANUARY 18, 2022
PAGE 3

5.  Fifth Amendment to the Franchise Lease Agreement between the City of Avalon and
  CR&R, Inc.
  During the January 4, 2022 City Council meeting, members of the City Council requested
  clarification and codification of specific information regarding the fifth amendment to the
  Franchise Lease Agreement between the City of Avalon and CR&R, Inc. çCR&R”). City
  Staff was directed to answer specific questions regarding CR&R and City operations and
  procedures and bring this item back at the next regular City Council meeting.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager to execute the Fifth Amendment to the Franchise and Lease
  Agreement between the City of Avalon and CR&R, Inc.

6.  CaiRecycle SB 1383 Local Assistants Grant Program Resolution
  The Department of Resources Recycling and Recovery offers SB 1383 Local Assistance
  Grant Program, a non-competitive grant program that will provide one-time funding to
  local jurisdictions to assist with the implementation of regulations associated with SB
  1383. The City of Avalon is estimated to receive approximately $20000 in grant funding.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt a resolution authorizing the City Manager to execute all documents necessary to
  secure funds and implement a potential CalRecycle grant to support implementation of
  SB1383.

7.  Fourth of July Barge
  The City contracts a barge company annually to facilitate the Fourth of July fireworks
  show. Curtin Maritime expressed their interest in providing the barge service for the
  Fourth of July show and offered to match the lowest bid received by any barge company.
  Additionally, Curtin Maritime offered to only charge for the hard costs and donate any
  remaining monies back to the City of Avalon to support youth activities.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager to execute an agreement with Curtin Maritime to provide
  barge services for the 2022 Fourth of July fireworks display.

GENERAL BUSINESS

8.  City of Avalon FY2020-2021 Comprehensive Annual Financial Report Fiscal Year -

  Ended June 30, 2021
  The City is required to conduct an annual independent audit of its financial statements.
  The audit firm of Davis Farr LLP conducted the annual audit and with staff assistance
  prepared the required financial statements. For the fiscal year ending June 30, 2021, the
  City received an unqualified opinion. The auditor is in a position to express an unqualified
  opinion on the financial statements when the auditor conducted an audit in accordance
  with the standards of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board and concludes
  that the financial statements, taken as a whole, are presented fairly, in all material
  respects, in conformity with the applicable financial reporting framework.
  Recommended Action
  Receive and file the Comprehensive Annual Financial Report and other audit reports for
  the Fiscal Year Ended June 30, 2021.

Due to health recommendations from the Center for Disease Control and State of California
Division of Occupational Safety and Health (CaIIOSHA), and the declared state of emergency
wherein social distancing measures have been imposed or recommended, the CITY OF
AVALON’S CITY COUNCIL and PLANNING COMMISSION MEETINGS SHALL GENERALLY
BE AVAILABLE TO THE PUBLIC REMOTELY. The general public may attend the meeting in
the Council Chambers however must adhere to social distancing requirements and wear a mask
or face covering at all times. The public is encouraged to watch and participate from the safety
of their homes while practicing social distancing.

Council Chambers are open to a maximum 30 members of the general public. Once the Council
Chambers reach maximum occupancy, the general public may participate in Oral
Communication and address the City Council on an agenda item in person by waiting in the City
Hall Court Yard and entering the Chambers one at a time at the appropriate time. No one will be
admitted into the Council Chambers who is ill or exhibiting symptoms of COVID-19. All
individuals entering the Council Chambers must wear a mask or face covering at all times.
Additionally, the general public may participate in Oral Communication and address the City
Council on an agenda items by providing comments via e-Comment. Please use the link below
to provide comments via e-Comment.

CALL TO ORDER- 5:00 p.m.

ROLL CALL-Present via Teleconference and In-Person:  Mayor Anni Marshall,
Councilmembers Cinde Cassidy, Lisa Lavelle, Michael Ponce, and Yesenia De La
Rosa. Also present: City Manager/City Clerk Denise Radde, Assistant City Manager
Michael Parmer and City Attorney Scott Campbell. Absent: Deputy City Clerk/Senior
Administrative Assistant Gabrielle Morones.

one written communication regarding Item #8 Fifth Amendment to the Franchise Lease

1.  Minutes
  Approved minutes from the December 7, 2021 regular City Council Meeting and
  the December 15, 2021 Special City Council Meeting.

2.  Warrants
  Approved warrants in the amount of $1736686.40, two payrolls in the amount of
  $373,771.71, five electronic fund transfers totaling $187,950.52 for a total of
  $ 2,298,408.63 for November 29, 2021 through December 24, 2021.
3.  Findings to Continue to Hold Remote TeleconferenceNirtual City Council
  Meetings Pursuant to Assembly Bill 361
  Determined that the COVID-19 state of emergency proclaimed by the Governor
  still exists and has been considered by the City Council in deciding to continue to
  have teleconference meetings and that state or local officials have imposed or
  recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID
  19, and that as a result of the COVID-19 emergency, meeting in person would
  present imminent risks to the health or safety of attendees.

4.  Development Impact Fees (DIF) Annual Report for the Fiscal Year Ended June
  30, 2021
  Received and filed the Fiscal Year 2020-21 Development Impact Fees Annual
  Report.

5.  2022 Waterside Permit Renewals
  Authorized the Harbor Master to renew the attached list of Waterside Permits for
  2022.

6.  Waterside Permit Application Taylored Catalina Charters
  —

  City Council made the affirmative finding that conditions set forth in the Avalon
  Municipal Code have been met and grant the Waterside Permit Application to
  Taylored Catalina Charters, with the following conditions: 1. All operations to load
  and unload charter passengers will take place on Cabrillo Mole floats except on
  cruise ship days when all loading and unloading will be from the floats on the
  Green Pier. 2. Applicant abides by the Standard List of Conditions for Waterside
  Permit Holders.

7.  Authorize Purchase of an Acoustic Water Leak Detector
  Authorized the City Manager or their designee to procure per the City’s
  purchasing policy an acoustic water leak detector for a total not to exceed
  $9,000.
 CITY COUNCIL MINUTES
JANUARY4, 2022
PAGE 3

GENERAL BUSINESS

8.  Fifth Amendment to the Franchise Lease Agreement between the City of Avalon
  and CR&R, Inc.
  Members of the City Council requested clarification and codification of specific
  information regarding the fifth amendment to the Franchise Lease Agreement
  between the City of Avalon and CR&R, Inc. (“CR&R”). City Staff was directed to
  answer specific questions regarding CR&R and City operations and procedures
  and bring this item back at the next regular City Council meeting.

9.  Discussion on Establishing Minimum Number of Nights for Transient Rentals
  There was no consensus to establish an annual minimum number of nights for
  transient rentals. City Council directed Staff to consider increasing the business
  license fee for transient rentals for the next Fiscal Year 2022-2023 Fee Schedule.

10.  Request for Proposal for Snack Bar Concessions at Joe Machado Field
  At the request of a member of City Council. Staff was directed to bring this item
  back for further discussion, The current tenant! Matt Affolder, reached out to
  Council asking for the RFP discussion to be heard again since he did not have
  an opportunity to address the Council at the December 7, 2021 meeting. Affolder
  had not been officially notified that Staff was asking to authorize a Request for
  Proposals for the concession stand at JMF, following his request to terminate his
  lease and for the item to be considered at the December 7, 2021 City Council
  meeting.
  Recommended Action
  Discuss and provide direction to Staff. Staff recommendation is to proceed
  forward with the authorized and published Request for Proposal and timeline for
  a qualified business party to contract for operations at the snack bar concession
  at Joe Machado Field.

Mayor Marshall adjourned the meeting at 7:41 p.m.

City Council Meeting on January 4, 2022, is the official record of the Council Meeting
and is on file and maintained in City Hall.

SUBJECT:  Consideration of a Planning Commission Resolution Recommending
  City Council Adoption of the Annual Growth Policy for 2022

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S):  Adopt a resolution establishing the City of Avalon’s Annual
Growth Policy for 2022.

REPORT SUMMARY: Section 9-12.102 of the Avalon Municipal Code (AMC) stipulates that
the City Council, in conjunction with the Planning Commission, shall review the growth permitted
in the preceding ten months, review the effects and demands of such development and any
additional development upon the City’s natural resources, and determine, by resolution, the
amount and type of growth the City will permit in the succeeding year, as well as City priorities
for growth.

A summary of loc& development activity during the past year (January through October) has
been tabulated and is attached as ‘Exhibit A” to the proposed attached resolution recommending
the adoption of the City’s Annual Growth Policy for the year 2022 by the City Council. The
summary also includes development activity for November and December as reference.

Southern California Edison (SCE) has notified the City that it is no longer under any stage of
water rationing. However, SCE has delayed issuing any new fresh water allocations to those
project on their waiting list until further testing of wells and quantity of production could be
ascertained. The growth policy being recommended allows the same type of development, but
has been modified to provide that almost all require confirmation from SCE that adequate fresh
water is available:

  •  The repair, in-kind replacement, remodeling or enlargement of existing commercial
  and residential structures: subject to specified conditions;
  •  In-fill projects involving limited new construction and subject to specified conditions;
  •  Residential tract development, if specified conditions can be met;
  •  An ADU or JADU is not allowed in any location within the City unless the water
  provider indicates there is sufficient water by issuing a water allocation or that no
  allocation is needed (Avalon Municipal Code § 9-5.605(a)(3));
  •  Infrastructure projects authorized by the City/Successor Agency;
  •  Projects which the Planning Commission determines will not have growth inducing
  effects; and
  •  Projects which are not in-fill in nature or involve existing residential or commercial
  structures but for which CEQA documents have been adopted and findings made that
  explain why the resulting growth is beneficial to the City and its residents.
 A project shall only be required to fall into one of the foregoing categories. The permitted classes
of projects are set forth in greater detail in the attached resolution.

The proposed policy does not constitute a project within the meaning of State CEQA Guidelines
Section 15378. Specifically, the adoption of the resolution is exempt from CEQA pursuant to
Section 15061(b)(3) as CEQA applies only to projects which have the potential for causing a
significant effect on the environment. The proposed policy does not approve any new project,
but establishes a policy for allowed growth.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: The proposed resolution is aligned with the City’s 2030 Vision and City
Council goals regarding Natural Resources and City Infrastructure.

FISCAL IMPACTS: None.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: Failure to implement
the Avalon Municipal Code mandate and continue to process development applications without
the benefit or direction of an annual growth policy.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Adherence to the growth policy when processing applications for land
use entitlements during calendar year 2022.

ADVERTISING, NOTICE AND PUBLIC CONTACT: Pursuant to the Brown Act.

   RESOLUTION NO. 22-

  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL
  OF THE CITY OF AVALON ADOPTING THE
  ANNUAL GROWTH POLICY FOR THE YEAR 2022

The City Council of the City of Avalon does determine, find and resolve as follows:

Section 1.  On December 22, 2021, the City of Avalon Planning Commission conducted a
duly noticed public hearing at which time written and oral evidence was considered regarding the
development of a growth resolution for the year 2022. Pursuant to Avalon Municipal Code
Section 9-12.101 etseq., the Planning Commission reviewed the growth permitted in the City
during the preceding ten months (attached as Exhibit A) and the effects and demands of such
development and other development on the City’s resources.

Section 2.  Exemption from the California Environmental Quality Act. The Planning
Commission has determined that adoption of a Growth Policy is exempt from CEQA under the
“General Rule” exemption, Section 15061 (b)(3). The policy is covered by the general rule that
CEQA applies only to projects which have the potential for causing a significant effect on the
environment. Where it can be seen with certainty that there is no possibility that the activity in
question may have a significant effect on the environment, the activity is not subject to CEQA.
The proposed 2022 growth policy does not approve any new project, but establishes a policy for
allowed growth. Staff is hereby directed to file a Notice of Exemption with the Los Angeles
County Clerkts Office within five (5) working days of final action.

Section 3.  The following facts were reviewed by the Avalon Planning Commission in
adopting the recommended Annual Growth Policy and form the findings of fact upon which the
Planning Commission adopts this resolution:

 a) New commercial construction and resort/vacation residential growth may contribute to the
  need for additional workforce, which in turn may create demand for additional housing.

 b) The demand for City services, such as wastewater treatment and saltwater service, public
  works, and police and fire services has increased without a corresponding increase in the
  funding for personnel and related infrastructure to provide these services.

 c) Southern California Edison (SCE) has notified the City that it is no longer under any stage
  of water rationing. However, SCE, in an effort to accurately gauge the safe annual yield,
  has delayed issuing any new fresh water allocations to those project on their waiting list
  until further testing of wells and quantity of production could be ascertained.

Section 4.  Based on the foregoing, the Avalon City Council adopts the following growth
policies for the year 2022, providing that new development will be permitted only for the following
classes of projects:

 a) Projects involving existing commercial and residential structures which are to be repaired,
  replaced in kind, or remodeled or enlarged, provided no additional bedrooms or dwelling
   units are added to existing residential structures other than inclusionary or density bonus
  units, and the Southern California Edison Company confirms in writing that water is
  available to serve the project, if approved by the City. As used herein, a replacement in
  kind is construction which does not change the prior use, increase the total square footage,
  or increase the number of units in the replaced structure. This section does not prohibit
  consideration and approval of conditional use permits for transient occupancy, subject to
  the limitations otherwise applicable to such permits.

b) An in-fill project. As used herein, an in4ill project shall mean:

  -  any residential project which creates five (5) or fewer units (including any bonus density
  units): or
  -  any non-recreational/visitor-serving commercial project that increases square footage by
  less than 50%; or
  -  any expansion of existing recreational/visitor serving development, not over 5,000
  square feet;

  and is on a legally conforming parcel, provided that if the project is not categorically
  exempt, then the project proponents can mitigate any adverse environmental impacts, and
  the Southern California Edison Company confirms in writing that water is available to serve
  the project if approved by the City.

c) Residential tract development of greater than five units may be allowed if the project
  provides 20% of the units proposed or one unit, whichever is greater, to year-round, non-
  transient, affordable housing and the Southern California Edison Company confirms in
  writing that water is available to serve the project, if approved by the City.

d) An ADU or JADU is not allowed in any location within the City unless the water provider
  indicates there is sufficient water by issuing a water allocation or that no allocation is
  needed.

e) Infrastructure projects authorized under or by the City/Successor Agency.

f)  Projects which the Planning Commission determines will not have growth inducing effects.
  By way of example, such projects would include non-inhabited uses such as industrial
  warehouses, mechanical, marine, or construction service areas and storage spaces and
  which do not create the need for additional employees.

g) Projects which are not categorized as in-fill or existing residential or commercial structures
  for which a Negative Declaration, Mitigated Negative Declaration, or Environmental Impact
  Report, with or without Mitigation Monitoring Program, is adopted and for which specific
  findings are made that explain why the resulting growth is beneficial to the City of Avalon
  and its residents and the Southern California Edison Company confirms in writing that
  water is available to serve the project, if approved by the City either via the existing safe
  annual yield or via an additional fresh water resource in accordance with SCE tariffs.

h) In any event, projects which have been granted a water allocation or water transfer, the City
   Council or their designee shall review and determine that water is available, and shall make
  an additional finding that any allocation or transfer of water for the project by SCE is
  consistent with the City’s adopted General Plan and that the allocation or transfer of water
  for the project is done in a manner that is fair, transparent, and promotes the public health,
  safety, and welfare.

A project shall only be required to fall into one of the foregoing categories.

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the City Manager or their designee to negotiate a
procurement contract with Al Larson Boat Shop, a sole source vender, for the Rehabilitation of
City Floats 2 & 3 for a sum not-to-exceed $249,999.00.

REPORT SUMMARY: On December 17, 2019, the City Council designated Al Larson Boat
Shop as a sole source vendor as defined in the Avalon Municipal Code to contract for repair
and maintenance on certain City floats.

Mole Floats 2 & 3 are in need of rehabilitation to extend their useful life and provide safe
facilities for the users. The rehabilitation is within the scope of work that is routinely and safely
provided by Al Larson Boat Shop. In 2018, rehabilitation of Float 1 was completed by this
procurement method. The proposed rehabilitation of Floats 2 and 3 will be the completion of
the planned rehabilitation of the ferry terminal floats. Timing of the work is sensitive to the
cross channel carrier schedules and opportunities are very limited to remove the floats for an
extended duration. Additionally, schedules are also sensitive to the capacity of the vendor to
complete the work, As such, City Staff contacted the cross channel carriers that primarily use
these floats and confirmed the Catalina Express and Catalina Flyer will be doing maintenance
on their vessels through January and February 2022. According to representatives from both
companies, the proposed January and February timeline is convenient due to the anticipated
diminished demand on these floats. As a contingency, Float 4 may be used for carrier landings
when necessary.

The Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal Rehabilitation (Phase II) may provide a major portion of the
funding for the rehabilitation of Floats 2 & 3. The rehabilitation of the ferry terminal floats was
included in the project scope under the grant agreement.  Under the Federal Transit
Administration’s procurement policies, grant recipients may use simplified procurement
methods for contracts under $250,000. Staff is pursuing this as a funding source, but the
logistics of federal procurements can sometimes be difficult for contracts of this type.
Otherwise the cross channel carrier fee increase dedicated to capital projects is intended to
fund projects on a priority basis such as the float rehabilitation.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Float Rehabilitation is part of our Capital Improvement projects outlined in
the Fiscal Year 2021-22 Budget (Project #207009). Approximately $260,000 is available in
fund 10470-6504 for this project.
 CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: By not following the
recommended project request, the City Floats 2 & 3 will not be repaired or maintained as
necessary.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Issue the contract to Al Larson Boat Shop for the Repairs &
Maintenance of City Floats 2 & 3.

SUBJECT:  Designate Al Larson Boat Shop as a Sole Source Vendor

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the Harbor Master to designate Al Larson Boat Shop
as a sole source vendor as defined in the Avalon Municipal Code to contract repair and
maintenance on certain City floats.

REPORT SUMMARY: The City-owned and maintained public floats present particular
challenges when it comes time to safely haul them out of the water for repairs or maintenance.
Additionally, due to the size, width and weight of the City floats! transport off of the Island to
mainland facilities is required.

Al Larson Boat Shop uses a unique rail system for hauling floats and vessels out of the water.
The vessel, or float, is ‘floated” onto a platform, blocked and secured, and then the entire
platform is winched up the rails to its final dry dock position. This is a safer, more efficient and
cost-effective way to haul the City’s floats out of the water.

According to the AMC Sec.3-4.111(b) Sole Source Vendors, “When there is only
one source that provides the necessary services, goods and equipment to ensure compatibility
with existing City services, goods or equipment, or the services, goods or equipment are
proprietary in nature, the City may procure the goods or services from the sole source.”

It is, therefore, Staff’s recommendation that Al Larson Boat Shop be utilized as a Sole Source
Vendor for maintenance and repair of the City’s floats due to their experience and ability to
safely and efficiently provide the requested services.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Unknown.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The Harbor Master
will continue to utilize the RFP process for City floats maintenance and repairs.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Depending on City Council action, schedule float maintenance and
repairs with Al Larson Boat Shop going forward, or continue to use the City’s REP process for
float maintenance and repairs.

SUBJECT:  Fifth Amendment to the Franchise Lease Agreement between the
  City of Avalon and CR&R, Inc.

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the City Manager to execute the Fifth Amendment to
the Franchise and Lease Agreement between the City of Avalon and CR&R, Inc.

REPORT SUMMARY: During the January 4, 2022 City Council meeting, members of the City
Council requested clarification and codification of specific information regarding the fifth
amendment to the Franchise Lease Agreement (‘Amendment”) between the City of Avalon and
CR&R, Inc. (“CR&R”). City Staff was directed to answer specific questions regarding CR&R and
City operations and procedures and bring this item back at the next regular City Council meeting.

City Council requested Staff provide in writing in the Staff Report and/or amendment:

1. What happens if the City gets the waiver for implementation of AB 1383?

Per Section 44.8 of the Amendment, “Meet and Confer”:

  In the event that City becomes eligible for a City-wide exemption from the requirements
  of SB 1383 at any time during the term of this agreement, City and Contractor shall meet
  and confer to evaluate potential changes to Organic Waste service and resulting cost
  reductions. Such changes and reductions shall be incorporated into an amendment to
  this Agreement and provided to the City Council for approval.

Additionally, per Section 6.6.5.5 #19 of the Amendment:

  If the City receives a City-wide exemption from the requirements of SB 1383 on or before
  June 30, 2022, it may terminate this Fifth Amendment with written notice to Company. In
  such event, the Fifth Amendment shall be null and void.

2. Who decides the fines that may be imposed for non-compliance of AB 1383 for residents and
  businesses?

Fines are established by the Avalon Municipal Code (AMC) Title 6, Chapter 2 entitled “Solid
Waste Collection.” Specifically, Section 6-2.133. Violation-Penalties, outlines the City’s authority
and process in issuance of a Notice of Violation:
   6-2.133. Violation—Penalties.
  (A)  Violation of any provision of this chapter shall constitute grounds for issuance of a
  Notice of Violation and assessment of a fine by an enforcement officer Enforcement
  actions under this chapter are issuance of an administrative citation and assessment of
  a fine. The procedures set forth in Chapter 1-9 of the Avalon Municipal Code shall govern
  the imposition, enforcement, collection, and review of administrative citations issued to
  enforce this chapter and any rule or regulation adopted pursuant to this chapter, except
  as otherwise indicated in this chapter
  (8)  City may seek all other remedies allowed by law, including civil action or
  prosecution for an alleged misdemeanor or infraction. City may pursue civil actions in the
  California courts to seek recovery of unpaid administrative citations.
  (C)  Penalty amounts for violations of Sections 6-2.128 to 6-2.132 are set forth in
  Section 1-9.03.

3. Who is responsible to ensure compliance of AR 1383?

Per State law, the standards established by AR 1383 were integrated into the AMC by Ordinance
No. 1204-21 on December 7, 2021. Per the AMC, § 6-2132. Inspections and Investigations:

  (A)  City representatives and/or its designated entity, including designees are
  authorized to conduct inspections and investigations, at random or otherwise, of any
  collection Container, collection vehicle loads, or transfer, processing, or disposal facility
  for materials collected from Generators, or source separated materials to confirm
  compliance with this chapter by Organic Waste Generators, Commercial Businesses
  (including Multi-Family Residential Dwellings), property owners, Commercial Edible Food
  Generators, self-haulers, hauler, Food Recovery Service, and Food Recovery
  Organizations, subject to applicable laws. This Section does not allow the City to enter
  the interior of a private residential property for inspection.
  (B)  The regulated entity shall provide or arrange for access during all Inspections (with
  the exception of residential property interiors) and shall cooperate with the City’s
  employee or its designee during such inspections and investigations. Such inspections
  and investigations may include confirmation of proper placement of materials in
  Containers, Edible Food recovery activities, records, or any other requirement described
  herein. Failure to provide or arrange for (0 access to an entitys Premises; or (ii) access
  to records for any inspection or investigation is a violation of this chapter and may result
  in penalties described in § 6-2.133.
  (C)  Any records obtained by the City during its inspections and other reviews shall be
  subject to the requirements and applicable disclosure exemptions of the Public Records
  Act as set forth in Government Code § 6250 et seq.
  (D)  City representatives or its designee are authorized to conduct any inspections or
  other investigations as reasonably necessary to further the goals of this chapter, subject
  to applicable laws.
  (E)  City shall receive written complaints from persons regarding an entity that may be
  potentially non-compliant with SB 1383 Regulations, including receipt of anonymous
  complaints. Contractors shall relay to City all written complaints they receive concerning
  acts or omissions of themselves or another entity that is potentially non-compliant with
  SB 1383 Regulations, including anonymous complaints.
 Per this section of the AMC, City representatives would include but not be limited to our Code
Enforcement Officers. Additionally, the City designee(s) include members of CR&R staff.

4. What are the fines?

Section 1-903 Cd) of the AMC assesses fines as follows:

  [jFines shall be assessed in the amounts specified by the Avalon Municipal Code,
  Resolutions of the City Council, or where no amount is specifically identified in the
  A va/on Municipal Code or Resolution, the fines are as follows:
  Øj.A fine not exceeding $100 for a first violation:
  L?1.A fine not exceeding $200 for a second violation of the same provision or
  permit within one year from the date of the first violation:
  [A fine not exceeding $500 for each additional violation of the same ordinance
  or permit within one year from the date of the first violation.

5. How does the proposed 24/7 system work? Who will be monitoring, in charge of clean up
  and when will the program begin?

Section 13 of the amendment identifies a Public Recycling Depot. Per the Amendment:

  Public Recycling Depot. In lieu of providing twice weekly collection seivices, Company
  shall establish a public recycling depot located at [insert address] where anyone can self-
  haul and deposit solid waste, Recyclable Materials and Organic Waste 24 hours a day, 7
  days a week, without charge. The City Manager may approve or direct adjustments to
  the hours of operation with written notice to Company.

The exact details associated with implementation of this aspect of the Amendment remains to
be determined. Upon execution of the Amendment. CR&R and City Staff will work to determine
an appropriate location and develop operating policies and procedures. The operations policies
and procedures will be provided to City Council before this aspect of the amendment is
implemented.

6. Further define the terms for dissolving this amendment if a waiver is obtained. Meet and
  Confer vs termination.

City Staff are working diligently, in cooperation with CR&R, to submit a waiver application to
CalRecycle from the organic waste collection requirements of SB 1383. The proposed
Amendment provides two options should a waiver be obtained:
  1. Termination of the amendment if a waiver is received before June 30, 2022, or
  2. An option to meet and confer with CR&R to renegotiate the Amendment.

The option to meet and confer versus a termination is established to provide CR&R and the City
the ability to assess operations and procedures that may be at various stages of implementation
at the time a waiver is received. Depending on the City Staff and CR&R would determine the
 best path to move forward considering what funds may have been expended by CR&R to date.
Any negotiation change to the Amendment would be provided to City Council for their review
and formal approval.

Additionally, the City Council expressed concern that the City would be paying more money for
ess services; however, CR&R’s overall services are increasing. Though the number of trips
seems to be decreasing from two a week to one a week, in reality, the picks will triple as CR&R
will send separate trucks for organics, recycling and trash.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: City infrastructure.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Currently, the Company Service Fee (Compensation) is in the annual
amount of one-million-eight-hundred-forty-thousand dollars ($1,840,000).  The cost of
compliance to implement SB 1383 will increase the total compensation by two-hundred-seventy-
six-thousand-three-hundred-three dollars ($276,303). The costs include an additional truck and
crew (at 50 hours) and additional residential carts, commercial plastic bins, and compactor and
service bodies to ship recyclable. Residential kitchen pails for organics will be provided by
CR&R, Inc. at no additional cost.

The anticipated cost increases were factored in with the Solid Waste service fees for five years
ending June 30, 2026 and adopted by City Council at its regular meeting on June 1, 2021.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: Chapter 12 of Title 14,
Division 7 of the California Code of Regulations (“CCR”) requires the City of Avalon adopt an
ordinance of similarly enforceable mechanism by January 1, 2022. While the City adopted the
ordinance at its December 7, 2021 City Council meeting, if the City Council does not adopt the
proposed Fifth Amendment to the Agreement, the City would be out of compliance for enforcing
SB 1383 and could be subject to enforcement actions by CalRecycle (the regulatory authority to
achieve the organic waste disposal reduction targets), including administrative penalties against
the City of up to $10,000 per day.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Notify CR&R, Inc. of City Council’s decision.

SUBJECT:  Fifth Amendment to the Franchise Lease Agreement between the
  City of Avalon and CR&R, Inc.

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the City Manager to execute the Fifth Amendment to
the Franchise and Lease Agreement between the City of Avalon and CR&R, Inc.

REPORT SUMMARY: On March 1, 2013, the City of Avalon (City”) entered into a ten-year
Franchise and Lease Agreement (“Agreement”) with CR&R, Inc. (CR&R”) for solid waste
handling and collection services. The Agreement was subsequently amended on June 18, 2013
(‘First Amendment”), on June 3, 2014 (“Second Amendment”), on June 2, 2015 (“Third
Amendment”), and on May 18, 2016 (“Fourth Amendment”). The full Agreement ends on June
30, 2023 and has the option for two additional five-year periods (the “First Extension” and
“Second Extension”). The extensions take effect automatically on expiration of the Initial Term
or First Extension provided each party has not provided the other with at least a one-year written
notice to not renew.

A Fifth Amendment was negotiated between the City and CR&R to comply with Senate Bill (“SB”)
1383 (Lara, Chapter 395, Statutes of 2016). In 2016, Governor Brown signed into law SB 1383,
establishing methane emissions reduction targets in a statewide effort to reduce emissions of
short-lived climate pollutants (‘SLCP”) in various sectors of California’s economy, including
methane emissions created by disposal of organic materials. SB 1383 establishes targets to
achieve a 50 percent reduction in the level of the statewide disposal of organic waste from the
2014 level by 2020 and a 75 percent reduction by 2025. In addition, not less than 20 percent of
currently disposed edible food must be recovered for human consumption.

To implement SB 1383, the California Department of Resources Recycling and Recovery
(CalRecycle) adopted regulations that mandate cities and counties to:
  • Provide organic waste, including food waste, collection services to all residents and
  businesses
  • Develop and adopt an enforcement mechanism or ordinance by January 2022
  • Establish an edible food recovery program
  • Update the City’s procurement policy to purchase recycled content paper and recycled
  organic waste products (e.g., compost, mulch, and renewable natural gas) at a volume of
  0.08 tons/resident
  • Provide outreach and education for generators, haulers, facilities, edible food recovery
  organizations, and municipal departments
  • Plan and secure access for recycling and edible food recovery capacity
   •  Monitor compliance and conduct enforcement
  •  Maintain accurate compliance records

Following negotiations, the following are a list of substantial, notable changes to the Agreement’s
Fifth Amendment:

Definitions

Container

This definition was added to define an approved container for disposal and storage until
collection of solid waste, organics, or recyclable material and includes a cart, bin, or debris box.

Food-Soiled Paper

Added a definition for compostable paper materials that has come in contact with food or liquid.

Food Waste

Added a definition for source separated food scraps and food-soiled paper (of which, food waste
is a subset of organic materials).

Generator

Added a definition to define a person who produces solid waste! recyclable materials, or organic
waste.

Hauler

Added a definition to clarify CR&R, Inc. as a hauler.

Organic Waste

Added a definition for organic waste as a solid waste containing material originated from living
organisms and their metabolic waste products including, but not limited to, Food Waste, Green
Waste, yard trimmings, organic textiles and carpets, lumber, wood, paper products, printing and
writing paper, manure, biosolids. digestate, and sludges, or as otherwise defined in 14 CCR
Section 18982(a)(46). Biosolids and digestate are as defined in 14 CCR Section 18982(a)(4)
and 14 CCR Section 18982(a)(16.5), respectively.

Organic Waste Processing Facility

Added a definition for a facility used by CR&R for handling! processing, and preparing collected
organic waste for marketing.
 Prohibited Container Contaminants

Added a definition that aligns the with 14 CCR Section 18982(a)(55) regarding prohibited
container contaminants.

Collection Services of Company

Container Coloring (Section 4.1.1) Labeling (Section 4.1.2)

Revised the solid waste container requirement to meet the coloring and labeling requirements
of the 14 California Code of Regulations (‘CCR”) Section 18984.7 and 18984.8 for the solid
waste, recycling, and organic containers. Labeling requirements include graphic examples of
materials accepted by the containers.

Solid Waste Collection

Single-Family Residence Service

Amends single-family residence service from twice per week to once per week and as needed
on an on-call basis.

Multiple-Family Dwelling Service

Amends multiple-family residence service from twice per week to once per week and as needed
on an on-call basis.

Recycling

Residential and Commercial Recycling

These sections were revised to only collect and transport unsorted recyclables and ship to the
mainland of California for recycling.  If recyclables and solid waste is comingled and
contaminated, CR&R reserves the ability to either no collect the material in the solid waste cart
or collect the materials and charge the customer for extra disposal costs.

The Material Recovery Facility will not be utilized as the requirements of complying with SB 1383
include source separation of recyclables, organic waste (green and food), and non-divertible
solid waste.

Construction And Demolition Debris

This section was revised to include all construction and demolition debris be shipped to the
mainland of California for processing.
 Green Waste

The subheading and subsections following was revised from ‘Green Waste’ to ‘Organic Waste.”

Residential and Commercial Organic Waste Collection

This section was revised to replace “Green Waste” with “Organic Waste and added that Organic
Waste will go directly into the composting grinder in the City. Recovered Organic Waste will be
used as compost or fertilizer and not alternative daily cover (unless the City receives diversion
credit).

Non-collection due to contamination

Revised the section to add that CR&R may collect contaminated Organic Waste as Solid Waste
and charge the customer for extra disposal costs.

Meet and confer

This was added as a new section, requiring the City and CR&R meet and confer if the City
becomes eligible for an exemption of the requirement of the SB 1383 regulations.

CalRecycle is currently accepting applications for waivers and exemptions from some or all of
the regulations for jurisdictions that meet certain requirements. Waivers are granted for low
population. elevation, or rural jurisdictions. For the City of Avalon, it can apply for a waiver, and
is currently pursuing one, from the organic waste collection requirements if it demonstrates that
the following apply:

  Low-Population Waivers for Cities that Provide Solid Waste Collection Services:
  o The jurisdiction disposed less than 5,000 tons of solid waste in 2014 as reported
  in the Disposal Reporting System.
  o The jurisdiction has a total population of less than 7,500 people.

Currently, CalRecycle records indicate that Avalon exceeds the 5,000 ton threshold. However,
this appears to be an anomaly as the City is generally below this threshold, and the City and
CR&R hope to get this re-characterized or otherwise acknowledged.

Generator Waivers

A new section was added for multiple-family dwelling and commercial customers to apply for a
de minimis and physical space constraint waivers as per 14 CCR Section 1898411. For de
minimis waivers, multiple-family dwelling and commercial customers can apply if one of the
conditions are met:
  • the total solid waste collection service is two or more cubic yards per week and Recyclable
  Materials or Organic Waste is less than twenty gallons per week of the total waste
   •  the solid waste collection service is less than two cubic yards per week and Recyclable
  Materials or Organic Waste is less than ten gallons per week, per applicable container,
  of the total waste

A physical space waiver may be granted to multiple-family dwelling and commercial customers
if they, or its property owner, provides documentation demonstrating that the premise lacks
adequate space for Recyclable Materials or Organic Waste containers.

Organic Waste Recovery Education and Outreach

A new section was added to the Agreement for CR&R to provide organic waste recovery
education and outreach. This includes education information on properly separating materials,
Organic Waste prevention, on-site recycling, composting, methane reduction benefits, how to
recycle Organic Waste, approved haulers, public health and environmental impacts associated
with Iandfilling Organic Waste, self-haul requirements, and edible food donation.

A new subsection was added giving CR&R the option of establishing a public recycling depot for
self-haul and depositing of solid waste, recyclable materials, and organic waste, 24 hours a day,
7 days a week, without charge.

Additionally, a new subsection was added to establish a contamination minimization program,
and requiring CR&R to educate customers (the public) on acceptable and non-acceptable
materials, monitor contents of Collection Containers for residential, multiple-family dwelling, and
commercial customers and conduct annual hauler route reviews to visually inspect contents of
Collection Containers. CR&R will produce written or electronic records and documentation of
inspections and maintain a database of SB 1383-related non-compliance incidents and
investigations.

The anticipated cost increases were factored in with the Solid Waste service fees for five years

 SB 1383 and could be subject to enforcement actions by CalRecycle (the regulatory authority to

  AVALON, CALIFORNIA AMENDING CHAPTER 6-2 OF THE
  AVALON MUNICIPAL CODE RELATING TO
  SOLID WASTE COLLECTION

  WHEREAS, SB 1383 (Chapter 395, Statutes of 2016) directed the California
Department of Resources Recycling and Recovery (“CaiRecycle”) to adopt regulations to reduce
organic waste by 50 percent from its 2014 baseline level by 2020 and 75 percent by 2025; and

  WHEREAS, SB 1383 also requires the regulations to recover, for human
consumption, at least 20 percent of edible food that is currently thrown away; and

  WHEREAS, CalRecvcle promulgated regulations as directed in SB 1383 in
Chapter 12 (Short-Lived Climate Pollutants) of Division 7 of Title 14 of the California Code of
Regulations (“SB 1383 Rcgulations”); and

  WHEREAS, the SB 1383 Regulations take effect January 1,2022. and requires
the City of Avalon to adopt an ordinance to enforce the SB 1383 Regulations by said date, and;

  WHEREAS, the City Council desires to amend its Solid Waste and Recyclables
Collection Services Ordinance to comply with the SB 1383 Regulations.

  NOW, THEREFORE, THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF AVALON
DOES ORDAIN AS FOLLOWS:

Section 1.  Chapter 6-2 is hereby amended in its entirety as set forth in Exhibit A. incorporated
  by this reference.

Section 2.  Environmental review is not required because adoption of the Ordinance is not a
  project under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)pursuant to CEQA
  Guideline I 5378(b)(5) (organization or administrative activities of governments
  not a project).

Section 3.  If any section, subsection, clause or phrase in this Ordinance or the application
  thereof to any person or circumstances is for any reason held invalid, the validity
  of the remainder of this Ordinance or the application of such provisions to other
  persons or circumstances shall not be affected thereby. The City Council hereby
  declares that it would have passed this Ordinance and each section, subsection,
  sentence. clause, or phrase thereof, irrespective of the fact that one or more sections.
  subsections, sentences, clauses or phrases or the application thereof to any person
  or circumstance be held invalid.

Section 4.  No less than five days prior to the adoption of this Ordinance, the City Clerk
  published a summary of this Ordinance in accordance with Government Code
  section 36933. The City Clerk will certify to the passage of this Ordinance by the

to the same terms and conditions as residential Premises as provided for in Article I of this chapter.

Waste. Recyclables. and Organic Waste collection services to business entities at each place of
business, the Contractor, which may or may not be the same Contractor(s) providing service under
Article I of this chapter. shall provide services to business entities at each place of business in the
same manner as collection services are provided to residential Premises in Article 1 of this chapter.

1383-compliant provisions of either § 6-2.212 or § 6-2.213. respectively.

SUBJECT:  CalRecycle SB 1383 Local Assistants Grant Program Resolution

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Adopt a resolution authorizing the City Manager to execute all
documents necessary to secure funds and implement a potential CalRecycle grant to support
implementation of SB1383.

REPORT SUMMARY: Senate Bill (“SB”) 1383 (Lara, Chapter 395, Statutes of 2016) was signed
into law in 2016. The law establishes methane emissions reduction targets in a statewide effort
to reduce emissions of short-lived climate pollutants in various sectors of California’s economy,
including methane emissions created by disposal of organic materials.

To implement 58 1383, the California Department of Resources Recycling and Recovery
(CaiRecycle) adopted regulations that mandate cities and counties to:

  •  Provide organic waste, including food waste, collection services to all residents and
  businesses
  •  Develop and adopt an enforcement mechanism or ordinance by January 2022
  •  Establish an edible food recovery program
  •  Update the City’s procurement policy to purchase recycled content paper and recycled
  organic waste products (e.g., compost, mulch, and renewable natural gas) at a volume of
  0.08 tons/resident
  •  Provide outreach and education for generators, haulers, facilities, edible food recovery
  organizations, and municipal departments
  •  Plan and secure access for recycling and edible food recovery capacity
  •  Monitor compliance and conduct enforcement
  •  Maintain accurate compliance records

The Department of Resources Recycling and Recovery (“CalRecycle”) offers SB 1383 Local
Assistance Grant Program, a non-competitive grant program that will provide one-time funding
to local jurisdictions to assist with the implementation of regulations associated with SB 1383.
The City of Avalon is estimated to receive approximately $20,000 in grant funding.

Eligible activities and project costs include:
  • Capacity Planning
  • Collection
  • Edible food Recovery
  • Education and outreach
   •  Enforcement and inspection
  •  Program Evaluation /Gap Analysis
  •  Procurement Requirements
  •  Record Keeping

Applications are due by February 1, 2022. To receive funding, Cities must submit a resolution
authorizing a resolution identifying a signing authority to execute all documents necessary to
secure funds and implement the program.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Fiscal stability.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Potential 520,000 in revenue to support the cost of compliance with SB
1383.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: the City will not be
eligible to receive funding to support the cost of compliance with SB 1383.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Implement City Council direction.

ADVERTISING, NOTICE AND PUBLIC CONTACT: This item was properly listed on the posted
agenda pursuant to the Brown Act.

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the City Manager to execute an agreement with

SUBJECT:  City of Avalon Annual Financial Report  -  Fiscal Year Ended

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Receive and file the Annual Financial Report and other audit
reports for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2021.

REPORT SUMMARY: The City is required to conduct an annual independent audit of its
financial statements. The audit firm of Davis Farr LLP conducted the annual audit and with Staff
assistance prepared the required financial statements. For the fiscal year ended June 30, 2021,
the City received an unqualified opinion. The auditor is in a position to express an unqualified
opinion on the financial statements when the auditor conducted an audit in accordance with the
standards of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (“PCAOB”) and concludes that
the financial statements, taken as a whole, are presented fairly, in all material respects, in
conformity with the applicable financial reporting framework.

The Annual Financial Report is presented in three sections: introductory, financial, and
statistical. The introductory section includes the letter of transmittal and organizational chart. The
financial section includes the Independent Auditor’s Report, Management’s Discussion and
Analysis (MD&A), the basic financial statements, Required Supplementary Information, and
other information. The MD&A contains a narrative introduction, overview, and analysis of the
City’s financial statements. It should be read in conjunction with the letter of transmittal. The
statistical section includes selected financial and demographic information, generally presented
on a multi-year basis. In contrast to the financial section information, the statistical information
has not been audited.

The other audit reports include the Summary of Audit Results, Independent Auditors’ Report on
Internal Control Over Financial Reporting and on Compliance and Other Matters Based on an
Audit of Financial Statements Performed in Accordance with Government Auditing Standards
(ICFR Report), and Independent Accountant’s Report on Agreed-Upon Procedures Applied to
Appropriations Limit Worksheets (GANN Letter). The Summary of Audit Results communicates
to those charged with governance (i.e. City Council) the scope of audit procedures performed,
significant findings, and other information, such as disagreements with management, audit
adjustments and significant estimates, that are not communicated in the audited financial
statements. The ICFR Report describes the scope of the auditor’s testing of internal control and
compliance and the results of that testing, as well as the City’s responses to any findings. The
GANN Letter summarizes the agreed-upon procedures performed by the auditors to assist the
 City in meeting the requirements of Section 1.5 of Article XIIIB of the California Constitution. In
prior years, the City has completed Single Audits designed to provide assurance to the US
federal government as to the management of federal assistance, The City was not required to
conduct a Single Audit this year as it did not expend $750,000 or more in federal awards for the
fiscal year ended June 30, 2021

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Meeting required disclosures.

City Profile

The City of Avalon is a tourism-driven harbor community located on Santa Catalina Island in
the Channel Islands, approximately twenty-two miles off the coast of Southern California. The
City’s jurisdictional boundaries cover a 2.8 square mile area on the southeast end of the island
 around Avalon Bay. The City serves a population of approximately 3,800 residents and
welcomes over one million visitors each year through its picturesque harbor.

The City of Avalon, incorporated in June 1913, is a general law city that operates under the
Council-Manager form of government. Policy-making and legislative authority are vested in
the City Council, consisting of the mayor and four council members, all of whom are elected
at large. The Mayor is elected for a two-year term and council members are elected to serve
four-year terms, with two members elected every two years. The City Council appoints the
City Manager, who is responsible for the administration of all City affairs and for the
implementation of all policies established by Council. The City Attorney and City Clerk are the
only other positions appointed by the City Council, with all other department heads and
employees appointed by the City Manager.

The City of Avalon is a full-service city providing a range of services, including public safety,
contracted through the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department, fire protection, planning
services, building inspections, and recreation and community services. The City is also
responsible for enterprise funds providing sewer, saltwater, and solid waste services, as well
as harbor operations.

Budgetary Process and Controls

The City’s budget document serves as the financial plan or operating guide of the government.
It establishes spending authority, describes the City’s goals and objectives and indicates how
resources are to be allocated. The City’s principal fiscal strategy is to present a structurally
balanced operating budget wherein recurring revenues exceed recurring expenditures. To
accomplish this, recurring revenues are projected using economic indicators, input from
professional consultants, and analysis of historical trend data, with conservative application
of revenue growth projections in an effort to avoid overstating available resources. The
objective is to then budget recurring expenditures below revenue projections and limit
expenditure growth to avoid excessive spending. Reserves generated by a balanced budget
can then be used to fund significant capital outlays and offset future revenue shortfalls.

The budget document must be adopted by the City Council after conducting a public hearing.
In preparation for this hearing, the budget undergoes a series of reviews and discussions with
the City Manager and key staff members to help refine the document. This document is then
presented in public workshops with the City Council. These workshops also afford the public
an opportunity to provide input during the budget development process. Feedback obtained
from these workshop discussions is then incorporated into the final proposed budget
document for presentation at the public hearing and consideration for approval by the City
Council. During the year, it may become necessary to amend the adopted budget as estimates
become more refined and as circumstances change. The City Manager has the authority to
move appropriations within a fund between programs; however, any changes that result in
an increase in the total budgeted appropriations within a fund require the approval of City
Council.
 In 1979, voters in the State of California approved Proposition 4, known as the Gann Initiative
to Limit Government Spending (Gann Limit). The Gann Limit places a cap on the amount of
proceeds from taxes that may be appropriated in a fiscal year. In conjunction with the City’s
budget preparation and adoption, the annual Gann (Appropriations) Limit is calculated and
adopted. The City’s appropriations for Fiscal Year 2020-2021 are well below the established
limit of $11,445,895.

Economic Outlook

With its picturesque harbor and as the gateway to the island’s open space conservancy, the
City of Avalon’s local economy is centered on the tourism industry. With a relatively small
property tax base and resident population, the City has historically relied on visitor-driven tax
revenues and fees to fund operations Visitors are drawn to the City’s abundance of unique
outdoor and ocean-based recreational activities, including kayaking, zip-lining, and scenic
tours. Shopping and dining opportunities are available throughout the City, with local
residents and visitors able to enjoy the natural beauty and warm temperatures year-round
along the City’s waterfront street.

The City is host to a wide variety of events, attracting visitors to the island throughout the
year and providing local residents with the opportunity to celebrate as a community, including
the annual Fourth of July celebrations, fall and spring community festivals, concerts and live
music, as well as marathons and other race events. The Catalina Island Tourism Authority
maintains a calendar of events which can be found on its website: www.lovecatalina.com.

Visitors seeking to take full advantage of all that the community has to offer and stay
overnight have a variety of accommodation choices including hotels, vacation rentals, and
camping facilities. Transient rentals are subject to a twelve percent (12°/a) transient
occupancy tax (TOT), which accounts for the majority of the City’s General Fund revenues.
Twenty two percent (22%) of the taxes collected are dedicated to the Catalina Island Tourism
Authority to promote marketing and promotional activities, with the remaining funds, which
represent the largest source of General Fund revenues, used to fund governmental services,
including public safety.

In addition to TOT, major revenues include Sales Tax and various harbor use fees. Sales tax
is the second largest source of revenue in the General Fund, with bars and restaurants
accounting for a majority of the taxable receipts generated in the City. One percent (1%) of
the ten percent (1O%) sales tax collected is remitted back to the City to fund governmental
services, with the remaining divided between the State, County, and various other agencies,
including a half percent (O.S°/n) to the Catalina Island Medical Center. The City is also
responsible for the maintenance and operation of the harbor facilities, which is funded through
user charges, including a three dollar ($3) per passenger wharfage fee, nightly mooring fees,
and a seven percent (7%) use fee on gross receipts from businesses operating within the
harbor.

The coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic and actions taken to reduce its transmission and
spread, including restrictions on non-essential travel, capacity limits to encourage social

  III
 distancing, and the closure of bars and indoor dining, significantly impacted the local economy
over the past two fiscal years. However, the City has benefitted from a resurgence in tourism,
particularly during the fourth quarter of the fiscal year, as widespread vaccine availability and
resulting reductions in transmission allowed for an easing of restrictions. TOT revenues, which
were down $893 thousand or 16.5°/o in the last fiscal year, rebounded to $6.02 million, a
33,7% increase from the prior fiscal year ended june 30, 2020. The City’s proximity to the
greater Los Angeles metropolitan area, its unique island location, and natural abundance of
open spaces contributed to stronger than normal levels of overnight visitors, particularly
during the fall and spring shoulder seasons, as visitors were able to enjoy the island while
working or attending school remotely. Taxable sales were relatively flat compared to the prior
fiscal year and remained below pre-pandemic levels, with overall visitor counts down as a
result of passenger restrictions and restrictions on the cruise industry, in general, which also
led to decreases in harbor operating revenues of $865 thousand or 10.6% compared to the
fiscal year ended June 30, 2019.

The City continues to benefit from the easing of pandemic restrictions locally, with cruise ship
visitors returning to the City in September 2021. However, the continued easing of restrictions
will lead to increased competition with other international and island destinations and it
remains to be seen whether the increased levels of overnight visitors experienced during the
fourth quarter of the fiscal year is sustainable. While the City has continued to see a
resurgence of tourism through the summer, the budget for the next fiscal year (Fiscal Year
2021-2022) includes conservative revenue projections and continued expenditure reductions
to preserve existing funds and replenish draws on reserves required during the initial response
to the pandemic. Additional information regarding revenue projections and insight on the
City’s economic outlook is available in the MD&A following the IndependentAuditor’s Report.

 Using this Annual Report
This discussion and analysis is intended to serve as an introduction to the City’s financial
statements. The City’s Basic Financial Statements are comprised of the following three
components:

  (1) Government-Wide Financial Statements, which include the Statement of Net Position
  and the Statement of Activities. These statements provide information about the
  activities of the City as a whole and present a long-term view of the City’s finances.

  (2) Fund Financial Statements, which describe how City services are financed in the short-
  term, as well as what resources are available for future spending. Fund financial
  statements also report the City’s operations in more detail than the government-wide
  statements by providing information about the City’s most significant funds.

  (3) Notes to the Financial Statements

In addition to the Basic Financial Statements, Required Supplementary Information and
Combining and Individual Fund Schedules are presented immediately following the Notes to
the Basic Financial Statements.

Reporting the City as a Whole
Government-Wide Financial Statements

The Government-Wide Financial Statements are designed to provide readers with a broad
overview of the City’s finances in a manner similar to a private-sector business.

The Statement of Net Position presents information on the City’s assets and liabilities, with
the difference between the two reported as net position. Over time, increases or decreases in
net position may serve as a useful indicator of whether the financial position of the City is
improving or deteriorating.

The Statement of Activities presents information showing how the government’s net position
changed during the most recent year. All changes in net position are reported as soon as the
underlying event giving rise to the change occurs, regardless of the timing of related cash
flows. Thus, some revenues and expenses reported in this statement will result in cash flow
transactions in future fiscal periods (e.g. uncollected taxes and earned but unused vacation
leave).

Readers of financial statements often ask whether the City is better or worse off from a fiscal
standpoint as a result of the current year’s activity. The Statement of Net Position and
Statement of Activities provide information in a manner that answers this question. In addition
to the financial information reported in these statements, economic factors (non-financial
indicators) should also be considered in interpreting the fiscal health of the government (e.g.
changes in the economy affecting consumer spending result in changes in the net position
and activities of the City).

  S
 Both of the Government-Wide Financial Statements distinguish functions of the City that are
principally supported by taxes and intergovernmental revenues (governmental activities)
from functions that are intended to recover all or a significant portion of their costs through
user fees and charges (business-type activities). The governmental activities of the City
include general government and administration, public safety, planning, public works, and
community services. The business-type activities of the City include sewer, saltwater, solid
waste, transit, and harbor operations.

The GovernmentWide Financial Statements start on page 20 of this report.

Reporting the City’s Most Significant Funds
Fund Financial Statements

The fund financial statements provide detailed information about the most significant funds
and other funds  —  not the City as a whole. A fund is a grouping of related accounts that is
used to maintain control over resources that have been segregated for specific activities or
objectives. The City, like other state and local governments, uses fund accounting to ensure
and demonstrate compliance with finance-related legal requirements. All of the funds of the
City can be divided into three categories; governmental funds, proprietary funds, and
fiduciary funds, which use different accounting approaches as summarized below:

  Governmental Funds Most of the City’s basic services are reported in governmental
  —

  funds. Governmental funds focus on near-term inflows and outflows of resources, with
  the balances remaining as spendable resources at the end of the fiscal year. These
  funds are reported using an accounting method called modified accrual account/ny,
  which measures cash and all other financial assets that can be readily converted to
  cash. The Governmental Fund Financial Statements provide a detailed short-term view
  of the City’s general government operations and the basic services it provides.
  Governmental fund information helps determine whether there are more or fewer
  financial resources that can be spent in the near future to finance the City’s programs.
  The relationship (or differences) between governmental activities (reported in the
  Statement of Net Position and the Statement of Activities) and governmental funds is
  demonstrated through the Reconciliation of the Fund Financial Statements to the
  Government-Wide Financial Statements. Because the focus of the Fund Financial
  Statements is narrower than that of the Government-Wide Financial Statements, the
  comparison may provide a better understanding of the long-term impact of the
  government’s short-term financing decisions. The Governmental Fund Financial
  Statements start on page 24 of this report.

  Proprietary Funds  —Proprietary funds are used to account for essentially the same
  functions reported as business-type activities in the Government-Wide Financial
  Statements and are reported in the same way. The two types of proprietary funds are
  enterprise funds and internal service funds. The City uses enterprise funds to account
  for its harbor, sewer, saltwater, solid waste and transportation services and uses
  internal service funds to account for general administration, insurance, and vehicle

  6
   maintenance. The Proprietary Fund Financial Statements start on page 31 of this
  report.

  •  Fiduciary Funds  -  Fiduciary funds are used to account for resources held for the
  benefit of parties outside the City. Fiduciary funds are not reflected in the government-
  wide financial statements because the resources of those funds are not available to
  support the City’s own programs. The accounting used for fiduciary funds is much like
  that used for proprietary funds. After the date of the dissolution of the Avalon
  Community Improvement Agency (ACIA) on February 1, 2012, the assets and liabilities
  of the former redevelopment agency were transferred to the Successor Agency of the
  ACIA (Successor Agency) and are reported as a fiduciary fund (private-purpose trust
  fund).

Analysis of Government-Wide Financial Statements

The government-wide financial statements include the Statement of Net Position and the
Statement of Activities. The Statement of Net Position reports the net position for

 governmental and business-type activities, as well as the combined total net position, which

Analysis of Fund Financial Statements

The City uses fund accounting to ensure and demonstrate compliance with finance-related
legal requirements. The focus of the City’s governmental funds is to provide near-term
inflows, outflows, and balances of spendable resources. Such information is useful in
assessing the City’s financing requirements.

The Balance Sheet for governmental funds is similar to that of a private enterprise in that
assets less liabilities equals the funds available for use. In the private sector, this balance is
referred to as retained earnings; whereas, governmental fund financial statements maintain
a Fund Balance. Over time, the Fund Balance may serve as a useful measure of a City’s
available resources. The Fund Balance designations pursuant to Government Accounting
Standards Board Statement No. 54 (GASB 54), Fund Balance Reporting and Governmental
Fund Type Definitions, are classified as Non-spendable, Restricted, Committed, Assigned, or
Unassigned. Non-spendable Fund Balances cannot be spent because they are either not in a
spendable form (e.g. reserve for inventories) or are legally or contractually required to remain
intact. Restricted Fund Balances are limited in use by externally imposed constraints (e.g.
debt covenants) or the law (e.g. constitutional provisions or enabling legislation). Committed,

  11
 Assigned, and Unassigned Fund Balances are unrestricted; however, their use may be limited
by action of the governing body (e.g. replacement reserves) or administrative purposes (e.g.
reserve for encumbrances). The Unassigned Fund Balance represents the resources available
for general purpose uses.

Major Fund Budgetary Comparisons

Required Supplementary Information follows the notes to the basic financial statements. This
includes budgetary comparison schedules for the General Fund and major special revenue
funds presented in those statements. These schedules report the original budget adopted and
final budget for each of these funds as well as a comparison of the final budget to the actual
amounts reported in the financial statements.

During the year, with the recommendation from City staff, the City Council revised the City’s
budget. Adjustments to the budget were made on an as needed basis to accommodate
additional appropriations and all amendments that result in an increase or decrease in the
total budget appropriations are approved by the City Council.

The City’s General Fund actual revenues exceeded the budgeted amount by $1.61 million
dollars or l6.4/o. Actual tax revenues exceeded budgeted amounts by $3.58 million, including
TOT by $2.20 million, sales tax by $646 thousand, and admission tax by $192 thousand,
Given the pandemic’s disruption to non-essential travel and tourism, the City had budgeted
visitor-driven revenues to be down approximately 3O0/n for the fiscal year ended June 30,
2021 compared to the fiscal year ended June 30, 2019, which was not impacted by the
pandemic. TOT revenues account for over half of the City’s General Fund revenues and actual
revenues significantly exceeded these estimates, particularly during the last quarter of the
fiscal year. In addition, the negative budget variances of $1.17 million and $1.01 million for
intergovernmental and other revenues, respectively, were due to decreased grant revenues
tied to reimbursable capital expenditures that were deferred in the fiscal year.
The actual expenditures for the City’s General Fund at year-end were $2.17 million less than
final budgeted appropriations. The budget-to-actual variance in appropriations was principally
due to unspent capital expenditures included in budget but deferred to future years in
response to the pandemic. The negative variances for Services and Contract Services were
the result of certain expenditures tied to revenues that exceeded their budgeted amounts.
For example, the City receives an additional 0.5°/s sales tax add-on revenue, reported as part

  15
 of sales tax revenues that it distributes to the Catalina Island Medical Center. Sales tax
revenues exceeded budget estimates resulting in corresponding pass-through expenses
exceeding their amounts budgeted amounts. Similarly, TOT revenues exceeding budget
estimates resulted in pass-through expenditures to the Catalina Island Tourism Authority to
exceed budgeted amounts. The City distributes 22°/s of its TOT revenues to the Catalina Island
Tourism Authority for the purpose of promoting tourism to the City. Lastly, the positive
expenditure variances were the result of non-budgeted cost saving measures implemented in
response to the restrictions on non-essential travel imposed during the middle of the fiscal
year in response to the pandemic.
